title: Chapter 180 – Jian Arrives
html:
[The Valley Wall to the Dock – Lin Jian]

They bury Lan Wen at the foot of the Wall at dawn, with the lamps still burning, and Jian does not cry until the earth is closed.

He had not planned to. He stands at the head of the grave with his staff in both hands and a blanket over his shoulders, in a crowd of Garden guards and Sect pupils gone silent with fatigue, and listens to Sera read the Roll. She reads it badly. Her voice cracks on the dates. When she reaches the last line, Captain of the Garden Guard, served fifty-four years, fell at the Wall, she stops and cannot go on, and a hundred hard-faced men and women look at their boots and wait. Han steps forward and takes the page, and finishes it in a clear flat voice that does not shake once.

Jian does not hear it. He is looking at the wooden marker. A plain slab of ash, cut that morning, with a single character burned into it in Lu Fei's neat hand: Wen. White. It means the color of a blind woman's eyes, and the color of the thing she saw at the end.

Find the nail.

He bows when the others bow. He lays a stalk of dried wormwood on the earth, because Qinghe once told him that was what you gave to people who had been kind and difficult. He walks away from the grave with his face composed. He gets as far as the shade of the Gate tower before his knees fold, and Han catches him under the arms, and he weeps against her shoulder like a boy.

She says nothing. She only holds him, a tall stern woman in a stained gray cloak, until it is finished.

"I'm sorry," he says into the cloth.

"For what?"

"For being the reason she stood in front of it."

"You were not the reason." Han draws back, and her gray eyes are hard and wet. "She told you so herself. A preference, she said. Don't take it from her."

He wipes his face. He nods.

"Good," says Han. "Now. You have a message waiting."

* * *

It comes by pigeon, in a tube of waxed paper, and it is eleven words long.

Gate opening. Yue at the bell. Pebble breaking. Come. Tian Mo.

Jian reads it twice. The handwriting is a cramped left-hand scrawl, not his usual neat square script, and the last word has a smear of ink where the hand slipped. He folds the paper very small. He puts it inside his tunic, against the place where his heart is running down like a clock.

"The Dock," he says. "Eleven miles."

"There is no way to reach it in time," says Han. "Not on foot. Not through that." She nods toward the south, where the pale tide still moves in the dim morning like the skin of a sleeping animal. "And you cannot fold it. You have not the strength."

"No."

"Then you will take the skiff."

He looks at her.

"It is the Sect's last," says Han. "A cloud-skiff, narrow, one-man, built for scouting. It flies at four hundred feet on a ring of light-stone. It cannot fight, and it cannot land under fire, but it is fast." Her mouth thins. "Lu Fei has been tuning it since dawn. I had intended it for a messenger. I think it will serve better for a keeper."

"Han."

"Don't thank me. Go and save the girl."

He bows. It is a very low bow, and Han returns it. It is the second time in four days that the Head of the Azure Cloud Sect has bowed to him, and he is suddenly and bleakly aware that he is being sent, not to a battle, but to an ending.

Make them good months, he thinks.

He climbs aboard the skiff.

* * *

It is a boat made of air.

That is how it feels. A narrow shell of lacquered wood no longer than a coffin, riding a ring of pale light-stone, and when Lu Fei pulls the lever and the ring begins to glow, the whole thing lifts off the stone with a soft hum and hangs there, trembling. Jian grips the rail with both hands. He is lying half-propped in the stern with the blanket around him and Bell's black pills in his sleeve, and the sky is a gray bowl overhead, and the wind smells of smoke.

"Hold on!" Lu Fei shouts. He is white with the effort of the controls. "It steers by lean, Elder! Lean left to go left! Do not stand up!"

"I had no intention of standing."

"And Elder." The thin face twists. "Whatever you do... come back. I recorded Gu's name on the buttress. I would not like to carve another."

Jian says nothing. He only raises one hand.

The skiff slides out over the Wall.

The valley opens beneath him like a map. He sees the whole of it in a single sweep: the Wall, a silver thread, with its row of gold-lit sections, and the dark patch at the ninth where Gu's keystone shines like a coal. The killing ground, strewn with pale bodies. The road, and the river, and the broken orchard. Beyond them, far to the south, the Garden Hall on its hill, lit like a lantern in a field of black.

It is the most beautiful thing he has ever seen.

The tide parts around it. He sees that from here, clearly: the great pale stream of the crawlers flowing north and east, away from the lit hill, like water around a stone. Qinghe's doing. He knows without being told. He feels a thin warm pride in his chest, so sharp it hurts, and he has to look away.

The panel hangs in the air a moment, thin and blue. He reads it with a flat eye and lets it fade.

Fifteen weeks. Plus whatever the Dock costs.

He leans right, as the boy said, and the skiff swings south.

* * *

The attack comes at the eighth mile.

He sees it first as a flicker at the edge of the sky, a tiny dark shape, wheeling. Then another. Then eleven. They are birds, or something like birds, great gaunt winged things with the long hooked beaks of herons and the skinless bodies of bats, and they come out of the cloud bank to the east in a tight arrowhead. Each carries a pale rider on its back.

Flyers, he thinks. Of course.

The skiff has no weapons. Lu Fei said so. It has a lever and a ring and a pilot's seat, and Jian has a staff and a failing Core and a mortal body that wants very much to lie down. He puts the staff across his knees. He breathes.

The first flyer stoops.

He ducks. A black shape howls overhead, and the wind of it flips the blanket off his shoulders. The second takes the skiff's rear rail in its claws and wrenches it free in a spray of splinters. A third rakes the hull. The little boat tilts crazily. Jian throws his weight left, and the ring flares, and for a sick instant the whole world goes sideways.

"Hello, keeper," says a flyer's rider, almost kindly.

He drives the staff into its chest.

It is not a good blow. He has not the leverage. But the end is iron-shod, and the pale thing grunts and loses its grip and falls past him with a long thin whistling cry. The flyer beneath it veers off, shrieking. Two more come in, side by side, jaws wide.

He folds.

It is a short one. Forty feet, no more: from the stern of the skiff to the back of the nearest bird. He lands in a crouch on its shoulders, in a reek of musk and rot, with the wind tearing at his hair. The rider turns its needle-mouthed face to him. He puts the staff across its throat and heaves.

They go off the side together.

He does not remember the fall. He remembers a sense of vast gray emptiness. He remembers the cold. He remembers the flyer, beneath him, thrashing; the rider, in his hands, going limp; the ground very far down, a dark green quilt, coming up with terrible slowness.

Then he folds again.

* * *

He lands on the Hall roof.

It is a hard landing. His boots hit slate and skid, and he slams into a chimney-stack with enough force to drive the breath from his lungs. For a long moment he lies sprawled in the cold with his cheek on the tiles and a taste of copper in his mouth, listening to the sound of his own ruined breath. The flyers are gone. They have lost him in the cloud, or they have more important prey. Above him the sky is clear.

Below him, in the courtyard, a girl is screaming.

He rolls. He gets his hands under him. He looks down over the edge of the roof and sees the Hall's great courtyard, lit by a hundred lamps, full of people. They are staring up at him. A white-haired old woman in a blue smock stands at the center of them with a kettle in one hand and her mouth open.

"Jian!" says Qinghe.

He lifts a hand. It is the best he can manage.

"The Dock," he croaks. "How far?"

"Seven hundred steps!" She is already running. "Pia! Get the stair-lamps! Tell Zhao the boy is back! And somebody bring a chair!"

"No chair." He is getting to his feet, holding the chimney. "I can't climb it. I'll go down the shaft."

"The shaft is straight down!"

"I know." He grins, an awful skull's grin, with blood on the teeth. "That's why."

* * *

The Gate stair is a corkscrew of stone, but at its center, behind a rusted iron grate, runs a vertical shaft the width of a well, dropping seven hundred feet to the Dock.

He takes the grate off with the staff. He looks down.

It is black. A cold breath comes up out of it, smelling of iron and old water. Far, far below, so small it might be a trick of the eye, a point of pale gray light burns. He has seen light like that. He saw it in the Hall of the Sixth Door, in the cold of a hundred sleepers, in the glow of a certain stored pattern in a crystal chamber.

Mei, he thinks.

He climbs onto the edge. Behind him, Qinghe is shouting something. He does not hear it. He puts his feet together and closes his eyes and reaches for the fold.

It is not a Core Step now. It is something else, something deeper. The Core is a burnt-out coal in his belly, but under it, in a place he has not touched since the root-hall, lies a thing Kito left him: a seam, a thread, a single vertical line running down through the rock like a plumb-bob. Kito walked it once. He folded seven hundred feet in a breath, and it cost him his life.

I will not pay that, Jian thinks. I will pay what I can.

He steps off.

The fold takes him like a hand. For one endless instant he is falling through the dark, through the stone, through the whole weight of the mountain, and he feels every ounce of gold in his Core scream and tear. He hears himself cry out. It is a thin, high, wordless cry, and it echoes up the shaft like the wail of a ghost.

Then he is standing on the floor of the Dock, in a blaze of blue light, and the cavern is on fire with sound.

* * *

The first thing he sees is the bell.

It is green, vast, hanging in the vault like a held breath, and it is singing. He has never heard such a note. It fills the Dock to the roof, a single pure endless tone that vibrates in his teeth and hums in the soles of his feet. The lamps shiver. The blue flames lean. And on the iron platform beneath the bell, a small gray figure stands with both hands pressed to a cracked stone and her mouth open in a silent cry.

Yue.

He starts forward. A hand catches his sleeve. It is Tian Mo, gaunt and one-armed, with a face like old paper. "Don't touch her," he says. His lips move in the roar. "Jian. Don't. It's the only thing holding the door."

"What door?"

Tian Mo points.

The Gate wall is open.

It is a seam, thin as a knife-cut, running up the black stone from the floor. Out of it pours a flood of pale gray light, and in the light, framed in the narrow gap, a figure stands. It is a girl. She is eleven or twelve. She wears a plain white gown too long for her, and her hair is pale, almost silver, and her face is small and grave and entirely without fear.

She sees him. She smiles.

"Hello," says Mei.

He cannot speak. He has never seen her. He has seen her pattern, a stored shape in a crystal, a flicker on a scan, a voice in his skull. But this is a girl, a girl, with a dimple in her left cheek and a grass stain on one knee that cannot possibly be real, and she is looking at him as if she has known him all her life.

"You came," she says. Her voice is high and clear and a little shy. "I told them you would. They didn't believe me."

"Mei," he says.

"Don't let the herd in." She glances over her shoulder at the tunnel, where the beasts are beginning to stir. "I can hold the door from this side. But I cannot stop them from the other."

He looks.

The herd has stopped. It stands in the tunnel, a thousand dark heads turned toward the bell. But the song is faltering. The Pebble is cracked from edge to edge, and gold light spills from the break, and he can see Yue's hands shaking. And behind the herd, in the black beyond the lamps, something is moving that is not a Gnasher.

It is a Rider, tall as a house, and on its back a pale figure holds a thin silver thread between its fingers. The thread runs back into the dark, a long glittering line, the Alpha's will, and it is pulling.

The herd turns.

* * *

He fights them for an hour, and it is the closest thing to joy he has felt in a decade.

He does not know why. He is dying. His Core is a cinder and his lungs are full of knives and every bone in his body complains at every move. But the staff sings in his hand. He stands in the mouth of the tunnel, where the Dock narrows to a throat, and the Gnashers come at him one at a time, and each time he steps and strikes and steps again, and each time a beast falls.

It is not the Core Step. It is older. It is the stance Tian Mo taught him, forty years ago, in a courtyard in the snow: stand. He plants his feet. He lets them come.

And behind him, on the black stone, Mei sings.

He did not know she could. It is a thin, high, wordless melody, clear as a flute, and with each note a fine silver light spreads from her hands across the floor of the Dock and climbs the walls and the ceiling and the iron scaffold of the bell. It touches the Pebble. It touches Yue's shaking hands. It touches the great green bronze above, and the bell's note deepens, steadies, changes from a scream into a hymn.

The crack in the Pebble stops spreading.

Hold, sings Mei. Hold. I have it. I have the weight.


He reads it with one eye, between blows. He does not look at her.

Let me, he thinks. Let me give you a week. A month. Anything.

"No," says Mei, behind him.

He nearly falls. He has not spoken. But she is looking at him, over the heads of the fighting, with her small grave face, and he understands that she can read the panel, because it is hers.

"I'm not a cradle," she says. "I told you. Don't pay for me. Make them good months."

"Mei."

"Please," she says, very softly. "I wanted to see you. That's all. Just once."

He sets his teeth. He turns to the herd.

And the Rider on its back, the great tall one with the silver thread, raises its head and speaks to him in a voice like cold water.

* * *

"Keeper."

It stands in the mouth of the tunnel, forty feet away, with its thread of silver and its terrible patience. Its beast has stopped. The herd has stopped. All the Gnashers stand with their heads lowered, as dogs stand when the master appears.

"We have not hurt you," says the Rider. "We have not killed the girl. We have been very kind."

"Kind," says Jian.

"We want only what is ours." The head tilts. "Give us the door. Give us the child. Give us what you carry, and we will go."

He considers. He feels, in the pit of his ruined chest, the thin cold weight of what Lan Wen left him. A name. A nail. A prisoner at the end of a thread.

"I know what you are," he says.

The Rider goes still.

"You are not the master. You are not even the Alpha. You are a hand on the end of a string. And the string is in pain." He steps forward, one slow step. His voice is even. "There is a nail in its heart. It does not want to be used. It has been trying to say so since the first night. I think it is trying to say so now."

"You are mistaken."

"I am not." He takes another step. "Lan Wen told me. She was blind. She could see more than any of us. And I am going to find the nail, and I am going to take it out. You can tell your master. Or you can tell the thing at the end of the string."

Silence.

Then, very slowly, the pale figure on the Rider's back lets go of the thread.

It falls. The silver line goes slack and drifts to the floor like a dropped ribbon. The great beast beneath it shudders. And all the Gnashers behind it, a thousand dark heavy shapes, lift their heads and look about them with dull astonished eyes, like sleepers woken from a dream.

The Alpha's will has gone out of them.

They do not attack. They do not flee. They simply stand, and then, one by one, with ponderous docility, they turn and begin to file back up the tunnel, the way they came.

* * *

The bell stops.

The silence after it is so complete that for a moment he thinks he has gone deaf. Then he hears the breathing. His own. The guards'. A child's, quick and ragged. And over all of it, a thin high laugh, shaky with relief.

Lin Kuang is on the platform with his arms around Yue. She is slumped against the bell's rim with the Pebble in her lap, and her face is gray and her lips are blue, but her eyes are open, and they find Jian's across the Dock. She lifts one hand.

Hello, she signs.

Hello, he signs back, and he is smiling, and he cannot stop.

You are late.

I was held up.

The Pebble in her lap gives a faint, tired shimmer. The crack across it is still there, a bright thin gold line, but it is no wider. It has stopped. It has been bound, he sees, by threads of silver light, fine as spider silk, laid across the stone by a small hand.

"I'll keep it," says Mei.

She is standing in the seam of the Gate wall, translucent now, her outline wavering in the gray light. She looks tired. She looks younger than she did. But she is still smiling, and in her face he sees something he has not seen in any face in many years: a person getting exactly what she asked for.

"I have to go back," she says. "I can't stay out long. It costs too much." She hesitates. "Will you come? To the tree? When it's time?"

"Yes."

"Promise."

"I promise."

She nods. "Then I'll wait. I'm good at waiting." The seam is closing. The pale light is shrinking to a thread. "Jian."

"Yes."

"Thank you for not feeding me."

The wall shuts with a sound like a sigh.

Nobody speaks. Then, from the platform, there is a clatter of boots, and a small figure drops from the iron rungs onto the floor and runs across the Dock at full speed. It is Lin Kuang. He skids to a halt in front of Jian, red-eyed, ferocious, with his wooden sword gripped in both fists.

"You're thin," he says accusingly.

"Yes."

"You look terrible."

"Thank you."

"Grandmother said you'd come back all bones. She said you'd try to hide it." He scrubs his face with a sleeve. "I'm not going to pretend I can't see. I'm thirteen. I'm not stupid."

"I never thought you were."

"Then don't lie to me." The boy's lip trembles, and he sets his jaw against it. "How long?"

Jian looks at him for a long moment. He could say a good while. He could say do not worry. He has said such things to a hundred people, and most of them believed him, because it is easier.

"Thirteen weeks," he says. "About that."

Kuang's face crumples. He does not make a sound. He only steps forward and puts his forehead against Jian's chest, hard, like a calf, and stays there.

Jian puts a hand on the back of his head.

"Thank you for asking," he says.

"I hate it," says Kuang, muffled.

"I know."

"I hate all of it."

"I know. So do I." He is quiet a moment. "But I'd rather be told the truth, by someone I loved, than the kind thing by someone who didn't."

They stand there, an old man and a boy, in the blue light of the Dock, until Tian Mo clears his throat from the floor and says, with great gruffness, that somebody had better find a stretcher for Yue.

* * *

Later, when the stretchers have come and gone, he stands for a long time in the quiet Dock with his staff in his hand and the lamps burning blue around him, and does not move. Tian Mo sits against the wall with his one hand over his eyes. The Pebble lies in a cloth on the iron step, humming faintly to itself. Somewhere above, very faint, through seven hundred feet of stone, he hears a bell ring in the Garden Hall: a plain, flat, joyous peal.

Thirteen weeks, he thinks. And a good morning, and a girl who waved.

It is, he decides, enough. It will have to be, and for tonight it is.
